A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pose Prior Learner work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison after matching reordered sections.

before.justification: v3.pdf reports original PPL keypoint-detection results, ablations, occlusion experiments, and qualitative analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v4.pdf retains these original experiments and adds reconstruction-loss ablation results, semantic-consistency examples, and classification experiments on Yoga82-Level1 and CIFAR-10.

M1.justification: The core pose model, four default losses, hierarchical memory, and iterative refinement remain unchanged. Appendix A10 adds a recognition adaptation: train one PPL per class, reconstruct each input through all PPLs, classify each reconstruction with ResNet-50, and select the highest-confidence prediction.

E1.justification: All earlier pose-estimation and qualitative dataset coverage is retained. Appendix A10 adds six-class Yoga82-Level1 recognition and ten-class CIFAR-10 recognition with clean and occluded evaluations, substantially extending task coverage into classification and general object recognition.

E2.justification: Table A5 introduces ResNet-50 without PPL as the comparator for PPL-assisted recognition, reporting clean and occluded conditions. Comparator membership in the existing pose-estimation comparisons, including AutoLink, Schmidtke/STT, and Hedlin et al. (2024), remains unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix A10 introduces a distinct classification evaluation protocol: a classifier trained on clean images, class-specific PPL reconstruction, top-1 accuracy, and random masking of 50% of a 16-by-16 patch partition. This adds a substantial evaluation design beyond keypoint detection; the existing pose-estimation splits, resolutions, metrics, and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table A3 adds an ablation replacing perceptual reconstruction loss with pixel-level MSE. Appendix A9 adds a qualitative examination of keypoint semantic consistency, and Appendix A10 tests classification robustness under occlusion. Existing prior, memory, and loss ablations and Human3.6m occlusion sweeps are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results are averaged over three experiment runs. The existing plots retain the same reporting, and v4 adds no seed information, dispersion estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests; Table A5 reports point accuracies.

E6.justification: New Table A5 substantially extends the reported outcomes: under occlusion, ResNet-50 without/with PPL achieves 76.5%/88.2% on Yoga82 and 72.8%/77.4% on CIFAR-10. Table A3 adds the MSE-ablation error of 2.84 and changes PPL-1MemBank from 2.62 to 2.72, resolving its discrepancy with v3's prose. Figure A8 adds semantic-consistency examples. Existing main pose-benchmark scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The pose-prior definition, affine transformations, connectivity formulation, memory operations, and loss equations are retained after section reordering. The new symbolic-prior terminology and reconstruction explanations introduce no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The original pose-accuracy, learned-prior, and occlusion claims remain. The introduction now identifies explicit symbolic priors as a separate contribution and frames pose estimation as a testbed for broader prior learning, extending the stated contribution beyond the earlier pose-focused framing.

C2.justification: Appendix A9 newly qualifies semantic correspondence as partial and not guaranteed. Section 4.1 explains that individual memory entries do not correspond to complete pose templates, while the recognition results receive a broader-applicability interpretation. Existing severe-occlusion and 2D-prior limitations remain.

D1.justification: The abstract changes from promising resource release to claiming availability through a repository hyperlink, although Appendix A3 still describes the dog-data release as future. Appendix A1 newly reports approximately 2.4 million parameters for the memory/prior-extraction modules, and Appendix A10 documents the recognition integration. Existing implementation settings are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds focused comparisons with Chen et al. (2020) and Guo et al. (2022), distinguishing their implicit structural information from PPL's explicit prior. Recognition-related references and citations for proposed future applications are added, while the existing related-work framework and established pose-method comparisons remain.

P1.justification: Memory reconstruction moves from Section 3.3 to 3.1, preceding transformation and connectivity. v4 adds focused explanatory paragraphs, Appendices A9–A10, and acknowledgements, and updates author information, publication headers, and the Section 4.3 title. Most existing prose and the overall section framework are retained.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn from a cyclic training/inference schematic into a two-panel learning/application overview and moved to the first page. Figure A8 and Table A5 are added, Table A3 gains an ablation row, and several captions gain lower-is-better indicators. Other diagrams, plots, and qualitative displays are largely retained or relocated.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens validation and reporting through the reconstruction-loss ablation, correction of Table A3's inconsistency, and explicit qualification of semantic correspondence. The recognition experiments provide useful additional evidence, but they train class-specific PPLs and give limited classifier-training details, so they do not establish broad transfer of existing learned priors. These are meaningful, bounded gains alongside unchanged main pose-estimation evidence.
